chapter: New Orleans ballrooms and Tony Almerico
title: Calling elders Mr. and why everyone said Jack for Teagarden
summary: Jones explains the habit of calling older people Mr., never calling Jack Teagarden anything else, and they note Jack's nicknames Jackson and Gate.

story.theme_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band monikers
story.community_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names

blocks.x: Anyone who was older than you was Mr. and if you grew up with them, I would have been a little bit more. And if you grew up with them, it was still Mr. if somebody was 15 years older than you. It was hard making the transition from Mr. Allen to Dick or Richard. Because it just became a habit. Someone was Mr. So and so. And I never did call Jack Teagarden anything but Mr. Teagarden. Now Addie was different, because everybody called her Addie, Mrs. Tebow. But to me, you just didn't speak to a deity on a first name basis.
Who did call him Jack? Everybody. Excuse me, everybody. The first time they ever met him they called him Jack? I don't know.
Yeah, I guess so. Yeah, I think so.
He was that kind of guy.

He was, I mean like when you were talking music and you said Jack, you didn't have to use the last name. Never. Because everybody assumed that it was Jack Teagarden, because that was the most famous Jack in the music business.
Nobody to compare. I've never heard of another Jack.

Yeah, I mean, not even approaching that level. And I think that's true no matter where you go in this country, if you say Jack. I mean whether you're in Jackson, Mississippi, they might think of Jackson when you say Jackson. That was one of his nicknames. Yeah. He used to call people Jackson.
And Gate. He did, personally. Gate. Gate was another one of his slang endearments.
